title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors
summary: Print processors are libraries that the print spooler loads to convert spooled print data into the format a printer understands, and attackers register malicious ones so their code runs as the local system account. Installing a print processor can be done through the AddPrintProcessor interface by an account that holds the load driver privilege, or by registering a Driver value under the architecture specific print processors registry path. The payload must sit in the print processor directory reported by GetPrintProcessorDirectory, or be referenced relative to that directory, and the spooler service must restart before the new processor loads. Because the spooler runs as the system, a registered processor grants persistence at every boot together with elevated execution. Detection targets the print processors registry key and the contents of the dedicated print processor directory, where files that are not part of a known printing product stand out. Correlating registry and file writes with print spooler restarts strengthens the signal.

beginner.definition: A print processor is a small program that the Windows print service loads. It turns your document into the data your printer understands. An attacker can register their own print processor so their program is loaded by the print service at startup.
beginner.whyItMatters: The print service runs as the system, the most powerful account on the computer. A program loaded by it gains that power. So one registration can give an attacker both a way to stay on the machine and a way to act as the system. Print components are rarely watched, which is exactly why attackers choose them. Small changes in printing settings are easy to overlook.
howItWorks: When a document is printed, the print service puts the job in a queue and passes it to a print processor.
The print processor converts the job into the data format the printer needs.
Windows records which processors exist in a registry key that lists each one by driver library.
An attacker installs a processor through a programming interface or by adding their own registry key.
The library must sit in the print processor folder, and the print service must restart to load it.
Detection inspects that folder and the registry list for files that belong to no known product.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital where every doctor's note is rewritten by a typist before it reaches the ward. The typist sits at a desk in the records office and works from a list of approved desks on the wall. Someone adds a desk to the list and puts a quiet assistant there. Every note now passes through that assistant, who works under the records office badge.
takeaways: Watch the print processor registry list and the dedicated folder where those libraries must live.
An application programming interface can install a processor, so registry changes are not the only route.
Because the print service runs as the system, treat any unexpected processor as high severity.

objectives: Explain what a print processor does and when the print spooler loads it.
Identify the registry path and the print processor directory used for print processor registration.
Describe the privilege required to install a print processor and why the loaded library runs as the system.
Detect malicious print processors through registry monitoring and directory inspection.
Explain why a spooler restart is needed before a new processor actually loads.
Distinguish print processor abuse from port monitor abuse within the same subsystem.
